editorNotes: Tinkaton is a top meta pick with its immensely powerful signature move, Gigaton Hammer, which even threatens Water types that resist it. Tinkaton shouldn't be phased by the Bulldoze rework, although it's difficult to crown amid that uncertainty. Its slower pacing will be felt, but is unlikely to shake it from its meta-shaping role.

Kanto Ninetales has quickly risen as a top pick with a Worlds-winning pedigree. Its Energy Ball coverage is so effective that it has warped Water and Ground types around it. The Shadow is almost always preferred. Ninetales struggles against Dragons and rival Fire types, so build your team accordingly.

Quagsire has the best bulk and pacing of its competition, making it a top meta pick. The Shadow is typically preferred. Its moveset has shifted between Mud Bomb and Stone Edge, with Mud Bomb making it stronger into Steel types and Stone Edge giving it coverage against Flying types.

Despite significant meta threats and a deep roster of Ghost types, Galarian Corsola remains a haunting staple. Its bulk is offset by a somewhat sluggish and underpowered moveset. A high rank Galarian Corsola has better neutral matchups than one with hatch IV's, so look to save your resources for the right one.

Corviknight receives damage buffs to both Air Cutter and Iron Head, improving its neutrals and giving it stronger identity. While its pacing is now slower, it's also less bait and boost dependent. It should be a strong contender going into the season.

Cramorant has a similar profile to Pelipper with middle of the road stats and well paced attacks. However, its special mechanics put it notably ahead of its counterparts. Gulp Missile softens its matchups and even turns some losses into draws. Like Mimikyu before it, Cramorant may see a wave of hard counters at its debut, so its long term viability may be unclear until later.

Melmetal shoots up the rankings with a major buff to Double Iron Bash. It gives Melmetal a 2 DPE attack at a blazing 4 pace. Dynamic Punch makes for excellent coverage as well. Its stat product is merely average and it may struggle against established picks like Quagsire and Kanto Ninetales.

Quagsire has the best bulk and pacing of its competition, making it a top meta pick. The Shadow is typically preferred. Its moveset has shifted between Mud Bomb and Stone Edge, with Mud Bomb making it stronger into Steel types and Stone Edge giving it coverage against Flying types.

Empoleon is the standout Hydro Cannon user thanks to its incredible pacing, Steel typing, and synergy with core partners like Altaria. Its lower stat product and struggles into other Water types haven't hindered its competitive success. The non-Shadow is typically preferred.
Mantine has become the Water type of choice to combat Shadow Kanto Ninetales. While Cramorant looks to eats a share of its usage, Mantine maintains superior bulk and broader coverage.

The Shadow is almost always preferred. Ninetales struggles against Dragons and rival Fire types, so build your team accordingly.

Thievul has had a strong competitive debut, making the top usage charts at Worlds. This season buffs rival Dark types, which Thievul struggles against, so it may have more competition but it's still riding a wave from its Community Day.

Altaria's flexibility with Flamethrower gives it coverage against Steel types, and its defensive typing remains one of the best to counter Water and Ground types. Altaria tends to see more play in GBL than tournaments.

Florges's mix of coverage gives it a unique matchup profile and technical play. Even Tinkaton hasn't stopped it from being a top used pick in competitive. Movesets can vary depending on your team and playstyle. Florges struggles against Dragons without a Fairy-type Charged Attack.

Corviknight receives damage buffs to both Air Cutter and Iron Head, improving its neutrals and giving it stronger identity. While its pacing is now slower, it's also less bait and boost dependent. It should be a strong contender going into the season. For those who find regular Corviknight lacking, Shadow Corviknight is worth serious consideration.

Empoleon is the standout Hydro Cannon user thanks to its incredible pacing, Steel typing, and synergy with core partners like Altaria. Its lower stat product and struggles into other Water types haven't hindered its competitive success. The non-Shadow is typically preferred.

Mimikyu's special ability blocks the first unshielded Charged Attack it receives; its Defense then lowers by 1 stage the rest of the match, even if it swaps out.

This effectively grants Mimikyu a third shield, a massive advantage that far outweighs its drawbacks. It performs best when given shields to delay the debuff.

Mimikyu's competitive presence has tempered, but still demands consideration during team building.

Jellicent has everything you look for in a top Pokemon - excellent stats, typing, pacing, and power. Its diverse resistances make it a centerpiece for team building. Its biggest flaw is its vulnerability to Normal types. Jellicent takes a dip this season  as Shadow Ball is weaker and Dark types are stronger.

Altaria's flexibility with Flamethrower gives it coverage against Steel types, and its defensive typing remains one of the best to counter Water and Ground types. It's seeing more play this season with the nerf to its nemesis, Wigglytuff.
Clodsire is never quite out of the meta and has always been a solid generalist. Its main drawbacks are its low Fast Attack pressure, pacing, and weaknesses to Ground, Ice, and Water.
Fearow's solid pacing and great offenses make it a top Flying choice in the metagame. While it lacks bulk, its Normal typing is highly valuable against Great League's resident Ghost types.

Furret offers a safe pick with Fast Attack pressure and coverage into Water types. With Lickilicky out of the picture, it's in a prime position to take that top Normal spot with recent seasons' success to back it up.

Vigoroth has returned to terrorize veteran players, this time with STAB Scratch as its Fast Attack. It will be scrapping for Lickilicky's safe swap role, with less bulk than other Normal types but impressive damage output. Rock Slide has been its coverage move of choice in the past, but it can make use of Brick Brick or Bulldoze, too.

Annihilape has maintained a small but constant presence as one of the lone viable Fighting types. This season, Low Kick should overtake Counter as the move of choice. Annihilape has multiple viable movesets, and must choose between coverage or closing power. Ice Punch has historically been preferred.

Annihilape has multiple viable movesets, and must choose between coverage or closing power. Ice Punch has historically been preferred.

Azumarill has withstood the test of time and remains one of Great League's most prominent mascots. It owes this to its extreme bulk and excellent defensive typing. Azumarill's main drawback is its pacing, which leaves it outsped by the format's more aggressive picks.

Our friend Malamar is a flexible Pokemon with decent competitive success. Quick pacing and reliable damage add to this Pokemon's unique typing. It performs best when Fighting and Poison types occupy the meta, which isn't often, and struggles into Fairies and other Dark types.
Marowak maintains a strong presence in the metagame even after the Mud Slap nerf. The non-Shadow version has risen in popularity thanks to its ability to tank Grass-type coverage moves.

Shadow Sableye has found renewed play with Drain Punch, of all things. This fast-paced Defense boost gives Sableye even more neutral play. This moveset is aggressive and technical, and requires significant practice to know which move to throw when.

Dondozo made a big splash at Worlds, outcompeting Milotic for a similar role. Its bulk makes up for its slower pacing and allows it to tank Grass coverage attacks. It's less flexible than other Water types, so it's better suited if you prefer playing for switch advantage.

Hisuian Electrode made a statement at Worlds with strong usage and performance in even hard counter scenarios. Wild Charge packs enough punch to threaten Kanto Ninetales, while Energy Ball devastates Ground types that otherwise resist its Electric attacks. It may not have the bulk or defensive typing to remain a staple, but this little ball is in the right meta at the right time.

Feraligatr is a longtime staple thanks to its powerful moveset. Shadow Claw shreds through ever-present Ghost types, and gives it a more neutral profile into other Waters. Preference for Shadow vs non-Shadow is split, currently leaning toward non-Shadow.

Guzzlord is one of the most viable Dragon types behind Altaria. Its Dark typing gives it the edge against Ghosts and popular Normal types like Furret. With Wigglytuff nerfed, it has at least one less nightmare matchup to worry about. Guzzlord's insanely high stamina stat makes it resilient to low-damage Fast Attacks.
Lapras has a long competitive history, but has been absent from the recent metagame. It's a poster child for bulky Water types and neutral play.

Mandibuzz is the Flying Umbreon with sheer bulk on its side. It's failed to break into the open meta as of late, with Tinkaton as an ever-present threat. Where it falls short in the open league, it's always looking for carrion in themed cups where it can out-bulk smaller rosters.

Umbreon stands among the bulkiest Pokemon in the format. While its top meta days are behind it, Umbreon has improved potential with the Charm nerf and Dark Pulse buff. Its biggest draw is its ability to absorb damage and grind matches to a halt, serving as a pivot or tempo reset. Its offenses are completely lacking, so pair it with high pressure picks for the most synergy.

Kingdra's typing gives it a strong neutral profile, but it lacks the bulk and resistances of more competitive picks like Altaria. Kingdra's niche is its dominating matchups against Fire types, which it double resists.

Kingdra's typing gives it a strong neutral profile, but it lacks the bulk and resistances of more competitive picks like Altaria. Kingdra's niche is its dominating matchups against Fire types, which it double resists.

Snorlax has reawakened with competitive pacing to fill Lickilicky's absence. It has has both Shadow and non-Shadow options to consider, and Superpower to lay on the hurt against other Normal types. Its matchups against Ghosts are more grueling, however.

Hippowdon is now a World champion Pokemon. It's comparable to Kanto Marowak with a 1-turn Fast Attack and better pacing to its Rock-type coverage. The Shadow version has just enough bulk to survive Energy Ball from Shadow Kanto Ninetales, but the non-Shadow is a bit more comfortable in this matchup.

Sableye is a longtime staple which has phased in and out of the recent meta. Tinkaton is a severe threat, so its traditional role as a safe swap is no longer safe. Still, its flexibility always offers a high degree of play. Return can't be regained once it's removed, so carefully consider your options before you TM it away.

It will be scrapping for Lickilicky's safe swap role, with less bulk than other Normal types but impressive damage output. Rock Slide has been its coverage move of choice in the past, but it can make use of Brick Brick or Bulldoze, too.

Blastoise is the bulkiest Hydro Cannon user and can augment this even further with Skull Bash. With an excellent balance of stats, power, and speed, it occupies a small but strong spot in the metagame.

Medicham may not be at its previous heights, but it's seen some renewed play, especially with the narrow Fighting roster. Its struggles against Ghost and Fairy remain, and its neutral matchups aren't as prolific as players remember.

Hippowdon is now a World champion Pokemon. It's comparable to Kanto Marowak with a 1-turn Fast Attack and better pacing to its Rock-type coverage. The Shadow version has just enough bulk to survive Energy Ball from Shadow Kanto Ninetales, but the non-Shadow is a bit more comfortable in this matchup.

Hydreigon has the typing to corebreak current meta threats. However, its double weakness to Fairy and glassy stats pose severe challenges. However, Shadow Hydreigon has proven itself on the competitive stage in expert hands.

Jumpluff can safely run its STAB moveset instead of its old dual-Flying set. With its extremely bulky stats, Jumpluff is a rare Grass type with relevance in the open meta. The non-Shadow is generally preferred since its moves are higher energy.

Snorlax has reawakened with competitive pacing to fill Lickilicky's absence. It has has both Shadow and non-Shadow options to consider, and Superpower to lay on the hurt against other Normal types. Its matchups against Ghosts are more grueling, however.

Carbink is the Fairy-type Bastiodon, but hasn't acquired quite the same notoriety or competitive success. Its slow pacing and prominent weaknesses make it difficult to use. It's seen increased usage to combat Kanto Ninetales and Thievul.

Dragonair is a fast-paced, aggressive pick. Despite its offensive strengths, it falls short of rival Dragons like Altaria, Guzzlord, and Kingdra in terms of bulk and resistances. Because of this, it hasn't seen widespread play in a while, but watch for it in Dragon-centered metas. The Shadow is almost always preferred.

Forretress has been a frontrunner in competitive play with great stats, typing, and coverage. The Shadow is typically preferred. Both Volt Switch and Bug Bite variants see competitive play. Forretress previously enjoyed Fire-free metagames, but Kanto Ninetales usage has surged so much that Forretress is in a riskier spot.

Galarian Moltres has seen better days, with a mix of meta developments pushing it out of the top Flying spot. Its stats are more tempered than Mandibuzz, so it has to watch for coverage and commit to shields.

Turtonator usually excels in themed cups, but has a niche as a hard counter to Kanto Ninetales. Overheat gives it closing power in neutral matchups while Dragon Claw is an option for more rounded coverage.

Diggersby is reemerging to contend with rising Steel picks, particularly Forretress. It's not best in class in either the Normal or Ground departments, but with its sheer bulk, it shouldn't be underestimated. The regular version is preferred over Shadow.
Lapras has a long competitive history, but has been absent from the recent metagame. It's a poster child for bulky Water types and neutral play.

Charjabug boasts decent stats and neutral play, which are hard to find among other Electric types. Its Bug typing softens its matchups against Ground types, and X-Scissor is highly valuable against Grass. Crunch is an option to hit back against the meta's prominent Ghosts.

Cradily isn't fully extinct, but nerfs and meta changes have pushed it to the fringe. Cradily thrives by piling Attack drops onto its natural bulk. It works best in the backline where it can make those Attack drops stick. Cradily isn't the fastest, so shields are important to block early damage. Cradily often dominates themed cups where it stands above other Grass types and other Rock types.

Defense Deoxys was a powerhouse in the early days of PvP, and is highly anticipated with multiple buffs this season. Sims don't capture its hit-and-run playstyle which clears its Attack debuffs. While it's hard to ignore the sheer numbers, Psychic typing is a disadvantage and Deoxys may struggle against the power creep since its heyday.
The sims don't always use Chilling Water optimally, so Alolan Ninetales should perform better in some head to head matchups than indicated.
Swampert carries a winning legacy since the earliest days of PvP. It has some renewed play, but is firmly behind Quagsire in usage.

Dewgong has a long competitive history thanks to its bulk and Icy Wind debuffs. It typically underperforms in the sims, where its full game effects aren't well represented. A reworked Drill Run further improves its pacing and damage output, making Dewgong a prospect to watch for.

Doublade has its share of doubters. Despite Shadow Claw, Sacred Sword, and amazing typing, Doublade has yet to prove its sum is greater than the parts. Compared to Aegislash, it's more reliable and less technical, but its higher floor also comes with a lower ceiling in terms of impact.
Dusclops doesn't see much play over more competitive Ghosts like Galarian Corsola or Jellicent. It's still viable in its own right, with great stats and pacing.

It's taken a while, but players are finally finding success with Aegislash in competitive. Its unique mechanics can feel clunky and take dedication to master. Mimikyu's debut hampers Aegislash viability, as Aegislash is completely thwarted by it. Before powering up, make sure to check your Aegislash's IV ranks in both forms.
Marowak maintains a strong presence in the metagame even after the Mud Slap nerf. The non-Shadow version has risen in popularity thanks to its ability to tank Grass-type coverage moves.

Seismitoad provides a shakeup as a new Water/Ground contender. It's neither the bulkiest or hardest hitting in that category, but it makes up for it in the sheer utility of Icy Wind. With a steady 5 pacing, Icy Wind is a direct threat to its only weakness (Grass), and throws a wrench into popular team cores.

Because of this, it hasn't seen widespread play in a while, but watch for it in Dragon-centered metas. The Shadow is almost always preferred.
Dusclops doesn't see much play over more competitive Ghosts like Galarian Corsola or Jellicent. It's still viable in its own right, with great stats and pacing.

Forretress previously enjoyed Fire-free metagames, but Kanto Ninetales usage has surged so much that Forretress is in a riskier spot.

Gourgeist is an alternate Grass option with its truly unique moveset. As a Ghost, it also operates as a solid generalist. However, key Normal types fill the generalist role better and threaten Gourgeist in return. Gourgeist works best as a surprise corebreaker with ample  support against Normal and Flying.

Grumpig's stats and typing are nothing to write home about, its Ghost + Fighting offenses are enough to make it a flexible choice. The Shadow Ball nerf will reduce its already meager usage.

Registeel is a relic from the ancient past. Its stats are still legendary, but it now faces a much stronger field. Registeel's complete lack of Fast Attack pressure means it must rely on Charged Attacks to KO, making it challenging to play. While it has some promising matchups, skepticism is warranted as modern meta picks can dance in circles around it.

It's been a hot minute since Talonflame has seen widepsread play. Since Water is a constant threat, Kanto Ninetales has become the ubiquitous Fire type. The new mechanics which prioritize Charged Attacks over Fast Attacks also hurt long duration attacks like Incinerate. Talonflame is still plenty viable, just not a top choice.

Meteor Mash gives Clefable strong play into other Fairies. However, it faces stiff competition and usually takes a backseat to more well rounded options.

Drapion sports neutral typing and a signature fast pace. Prominent Steel types keep it from achieving its past potential. Shadow Drapion is typically preferred over the normal version.

Samurott looks great on paper, and while it's by no means a bad pick, it lacks the competitive success and neutral play of its peers. Its Bug offenses are its main detriment and are widely resisted by the main meta players.

Hydreigon has the typing to corebreak current meta threats. However, its double weakness to Fairy and glassy stats pose severe challenges. However, Shadow Hydreigon has proven itself on the competitive stage in expert hands.

Oranguru has solid stats and a neutral type profile. Confusion gives it a clunky playstyle. It's frequently a top pick in themed cups, but doesn't see play in open competition, where Psychic damage is less valuable and it's eclipsed by other Normal types.

Thunder Fang plus debuffing attacks give Steelix a unique role. The Shadow boost helps make up for its lack of STAB, but it still struggles with its minimal shield pressure and closing power. Look to pair it with strong offensive pressure and Pokemon that can capitalize on alignment.

The new mechanics which prioritize Charged Attacks over Fast Attacks also hurt long duration attacks like Incinerate. Talonflame is still plenty viable, just not a top choice.
While Wigglytuff's neutral matchups are dialed back, the hard counter role it's known for still remains. It's better suited for themed cups now than open competition.

Walrein has a notable competitive past, but hasn't found a way to crack the current metagame. Its time may come again, but faces too much competition against rival Water types, including its pre-evolution, Sealeo.

Spiritomb sees far less play than its counterpart, Sableye. Its pacing is considerably slow in a meta that is growing ever faster. In particular, this means it can't take full advantage of Rock Tomb's debuffs.
Guzzlord is preferred over Zweilous with its slightly better stats and Poison coverage into Fairy counters.
Metang has good stats and pacing, but has struggled to find competitive success. It struggles significantly against rival Steel types, and its Psychic typing makes it vulnerable to prevalent Ghosts.

Shadow Steelix is typically preferred over the regular variant for additional Fast Attack pressure and the boost to its non-STAB attacks.

Bastiodon is seemingly extinct after a long reign of terror. It's the sheer definition of bulk with a win hard, lose hard playstyle. The metagame has turbocharged ahead of it, so it'll need a major revival to see contention.
